A tariff is a tax that a government charges on goods that are brought into the country from abroad.

That's the heart of it. When a business in one country imports a product — steel, wheat, cars, clothes, electronics — the government of the importing country may demand a payment at the border before allowing that product to come in. That payment is the tariff.

The word "tariff" and the word "tax" are very close in meaning in this context. The key distinction is that a regular tax (like income tax) is charged to people and businesses within a country. A tariff is specifically a tax on goods crossing a national border, typically when entering the country.

Imagine India imports a ton of steel from China. If India has placed a 20% tariff on imported steel, then when that steel arrives at an Indian port, the Indian importer must pay the government 20% of the steel's value before it can be cleared through customs and used or sold.

The tariff is collected at the point of entry — usually at ports, airports, or land borders — by the customs authority of the country.
The Two Main Kinds of Tariffs

1. Ad valorem tariff — This is calculated as a percentage of the value of the imported good.

  • Example: A 15% tariff on imported cars. If a car is worth ₹20 lakh, the importer pays ₹3 lakh as tariff.

2. Specific tariff — This is a fixed amount per unit, regardless of value.

  • Example: ₹500 per kilogram of imported sugar, no matter what the market price of sugar is.

Sometimes both are combined into what's called a compound tariff — a percentage plus a fixed amount per unit.

Governments don't impose tariffs randomly. There are well-established reasons:

1. To protect domestic industries
This is the most common reason. When foreign companies can produce goods more cheaply (because of cheaper labour, raw materials, or government subsidies in their own country), domestic producers struggle to compete. A tariff makes the imported version more expensive, giving local businesses a fairer chance.

For example, if imported Chinese solar panels are very cheap, an Indian solar panel manufacturer might go out of business because nobody would buy the more expensive Indian version. A tariff on Chinese panels makes them pricier, levelling the playing field.

2. To earn government revenue
Every tariff collected goes into the government's treasury. For many developing and smaller countries, tariffs are a significant source of income, since they're easier to collect at borders than tracking all domestic economic activity.

3. To protect "infant industries"
When a country is trying to build up a brand-new industry that doesn't yet exist domestically, tariffs can shield it from full foreign competition until it matures and becomes self-sufficient. The logic: give it time to grow, then remove the protection gradually.

4. As a tool in trade negotiations and disputes
Countries use tariffs as leverage. If Country A feels Country B is trading unfairly, it might threaten to — or actually — impose tariffs on B's goods. This is a form of economic pressure. This is what a trade war is: two or more countries escalating tariffs against each other's goods in retaliation.

5. For national security
A country may decide that certain industries — like food production, steel manufacturing, or defence equipment — must be preserved domestically, even if it's cheaper to import. If the country becomes too dependent on another nation for essential goods, it becomes vulnerable. Tariffs keep those industries alive at home.

6. To correct a trade imbalance
If a country is importing far more than it's exporting (a trade deficit), tariffs can be used to curb imports and push citizens toward buying locally made goods.
The Real-World Effects of a Tariff

Understanding who gains and who loses when a tariff is imposed is crucial.

Domestic producers gain — They face less foreign competition, so they can sell more and sometimes charge higher prices.

Consumers lose — Imported goods become more expensive. And because domestic producers now face less pressure, they may also raise their prices. The ordinary person often pays more for the same product.

The government gains — It collects the tariff revenue.

Foreign exporters lose — Their goods become more expensive in the tariff-imposing country, so they sell less there.

Overall economic efficiency can decline — Free trade generally allows each country to produce what it's best at and trade for the rest, which keeps prices low and quality high globally. Tariffs disrupt this, sometimes protecting inefficient domestic industries at the cost of higher prices for everyone.
Tariffs vs. Other Trade Barriers (Important Distinctions)

It helps to understand what tariffs are not, so you don't confuse them with similar concepts:

Tariff vs. Quota: A quota is a limit on the quantity of a good that can be imported, regardless of price. A tariff lets any amount come in — but makes it more expensive. A quota physically restricts volume; a tariff restricts via cost.

Tariff vs. Embargo: An embargo is a complete ban on trade with a particular country, usually for political or security reasons. A tariff doesn't ban anything — it just taxes it.

Tariff vs. Subsidy: A subsidy is money the government gives to domestic producers to help them compete. A tariff, by contrast, makes foreign goods more expensive rather than making domestic goods cheaper. Both achieve a similar protective effect, but through opposite mechanisms.
Tariff Rates: How High or Low?

Tariff rates vary enormously — from 0% (meaning no tariff at all, common between countries in a free trade agreement) to well over 100% on certain sensitive goods. For instance, some countries impose very high tariffs on agricultural products like rice or sugar to protect their farmers.

When countries join a free trade agreement (FTA) or a bloc like the European Union or ASEAN, they typically agree to reduce or eliminate tariffs among themselves — while still potentially maintaining tariffs on goods from outside the bloc.

The collective average tariff level a country charges is sometimes called its tariff wall — a metaphor for how high the barrier is to incoming foreign trade.
A Quick, Grounded Example to Tie It All Together

Suppose the US imposes a 25% tariff on imported steel.

  • A US company that uses steel to build cars now pays more for imported steel.
  • This pushes the company to buy from US steel producers instead (domestic producers benefit).
  • But it also raises the cost of making cars in the US, which means US car buyers may pay more (consumers lose).
  • Meanwhile, foreign steel exporters sell less steel in the US (foreign producers lose).
  • The US government collects tariff revenue on whatever steel is still imported (government gains).
  • Other steel-exporting countries may retaliate with their own tariffs on US goods (trade war risk).

This is exactly what happened during the US–China trade disputes starting in 2018 — both countries imposed round after round of tariffs on each other's goods, affecting industries ranging from soybeans to semiconductors.

A tariff is a government-imposed tax on imported goods, collected at the border. It makes foreign products more expensive, which can protect domestic industries and earn government revenue, but typically raises prices for consumers and can trigger trade conflicts. It is one of the oldest and most widely used tools of trade policy, sitting at the centre of ongoing debates between free trade (let goods flow without barriers for maximum efficiency and low prices) and protectionism (shield domestic industries even at some cost to efficiency).
